literature.headline_zh: 人偏肺病毒本期文献呈现多方向研究进展
literature.lead_zh: 本期人偏肺病毒研究集中呈现以下进展。
key_findings_zh: 接受 IVX-A12 的 25 名(35.2%)参与者和接受 RSVPreF3 的 36 名(50.0%)参与者发生了不良反应。分别有 5 名 (7.0%) 和 11 名 (15.3%) 参与者报告了未经请求的不良事件。2 名 (2.8%) 和 1 名 (1.4%) 参与者观察到严重不良事件,而 1 名 (1.4%) 和 9 名 (12.5%) 参与者报告了医疗处理的不良事件。 [10.1093/infdis/jiag531]
抗原测试的敏感性范围为 20.6%(腺病毒)至 79.7%(hMPV),而所有六个目标的特异性均超过 99%,总体一致性范围为 90.7% 至 99.0%。对于每种病毒,抗原检测阳性率随着病毒载量的增加而急剧增加,在病毒载量≥10^6–10^7拷贝/100μL时接近90–100%,在病毒载量≤10^4–10^5拷贝/100μL时下降到50%以下。 [10.1128/jcm.00964-26]
该模型表现出良好的区分度,验证数据集上的曲线下面积为 0.78。结论 在因 WHO 定义的肺炎入院的儿童中,对各种生物标志物和临床表现进行建模仍然无法以足够的准确性区分细菌性肺炎和病毒性肺炎,以指导临床管理。 [PMCID:PMC13727722]
我们证明了 HMPV N 与选择性自噬机制的两个关键组成部分 TAX1BP1 和 LC3 相互作用。 [10.3390/biom16111588]
3601 份样本中的 303 份(8.4%)检测到 RSV,其中 5.9% 的 RSV 阳性成年人同时感染,主要是鼻病毒 (RV) 和流感病毒 (IFV)。 [PMCID:PMC13728999]
literature.trend_or_risk_zh: 本期研究方向以入选文献实际覆盖的临床、流行病学、宿主生态、诊断或分子监测主题为准。

Sensitivity of the antigen tests ranged from 20.6% (adenovirus) to 79.7% (hMPV), while specificity exceeded 99% for all six targets and overall agreement ranged from 90.7% to 99.0%. [10.1128/jcm.00964-26]

This model demonstrated good discrimination, with an Area Under the Curve of 0.78 on the validation dataset.ConclusionAmong children admitted to the hospital with WHO-defined pneumonia, modelling a wide range of biomarkers and clinical presentations still failed to distinguish bacterial from viral pneumonia with enough accuracy to guide clinical management. [PMCID:PMC13727722]
We demonstrated that HMPV N interacts with TAX1BP1 and LC3, two key components of the selective autophagy machinery. [10.3390/biom16111588]
Human metapneumovirus (hMPV; n=124, 27.1%) and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV; n=85, 18.6%) were the most frequently detected pathogens among the 457 pneumonia cases. [10.7883/yoken.jjid.2026.117]

papers.title: A Phase 2 Trial of a Respiratory Syncytial Virus and Human Metapneumovirus Combination Virus-Like Particle Vaccine IVX-A12 in Adults ≥60 Years of Age
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Older adults (≥60 years) are susceptible to severe outcomes from infection with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) or human metapneumovirus (hMPV). IVX-A12 is an investigational vaccine that uses virus-like particles (VLPs) to elicit an immune response against RSV and hMPV. Methods This Phase 2 trial (NCT06481579) randomized (1:1) adults ≥60 years of age to receive a single dose of IVX-A12 (150 μg RSV/150 μg hMPV) or the licensed RSV vaccine RSVPreF3 120 μg with AS01E adjuvant. Safety and immunogenicity were evaluated through 180 days post-vaccination. Results Overall, 143 participants received IVX-A12 (n = 71) or RSVPreF3 (n = 72). Solicited adverse reactions were reported through 7 days post-vaccination (IVX-A12, 25 [35.2%]; RSVPreF3, 36 [50.0%]). Unsolicited adverse events (AEs) were collected through Day 29 (IVX-A12, 5 [7.0%]; RSVPreF3, 11 [15.3%]). Serious AEs (IVX-A12, 2 [2.8%]; RSVPreF3, 1 [1.4%]) and medically attended AEs (IVX-A12, 1 [1.4%]; RSVPreF3, 9 [12.5%]) were documented through Day 181. There were no AEs of special interest and AEs leading to study discontinuation. At Day 29, IVX-A12 and RSVPreF3 administration increased RSV A neutralizing antibody (nAb) levels with geometric mean fold rise (GMFR) of 3.4 and 6.5, and RSV B nAb levels with GMFR of 2.9 and 5.4, respectively. IVX-A12, but not RSVPreF3, also increased hMPV A (GMFR 3.0) and hMPV B (GMFR 2.9) nAb levels. Conclusions IVX-A12 and RSVPreF3 were well tolerated and elicited nAb responses against their targeted pathogens. Given the neutralizing antibody response following IVX-A12, further investigation of an RSV-hMPV VLP combination vaccine is warranted.

source_records.abstract: BACKGROUND: Older adults (≥60 years) are susceptible to severe outcomes from infection with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) or human metapneumovirus (hMPV). IVX-A12 is an investigational vaccine that uses virus-like particles (VLPs) to elicit an immune response against RSV and hMPV. METHODS: This Phase 2 trial (NCT06481579) randomized (1:1) adults ≥60 years of age to receive a single dose of IVX-A12 (150 μg RSV/150 μg hMPV) or the licensed RSV vaccine RSVPreF3 120 μg with AS01E adjuvant. Unsolicited adverse events (AEs) were collected through Day 29 (IVX-A12, 5 [7.0%]; RSVPreF3, 11 [15.3%]). Serious AEs (IVX-A12, 2 [2.8%]; RSVPreF3, 1 [1.4%]) and medically attended AEs (IVX-A12, 1 [1.4%]; RSVPreF3, 9 [12.5%]) were documented through Day 181. Given the neutralizing antibody response following IVX-A12, further investigation of an RSV-hMPV VLP combination vaccine is warranted.

papers.title: Diagnostic performance of antigen-based rapid test kits for six respiratory viruses in children: comparison with a multiplex PCR panel and correlation with viral load.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Rapid antigen tests are widely used for point-of-care diagnosis of respiratory tract infection (RTI) in children, but how the sensitivity is influenced by viral load has not been comprehensively characterized across multiple pediatric respiratory viruses. In this prospective, paired-specimen study conducted at the pediatric center, two simultaneous nasopharyngeal swabs were obtained from children with RTI. One swab was tested using antigen-based rapid test kits (ImunoAce series, Tauns Laboratories, Inc.) for SARS-CoV-2, influenza A, influenza B, adenovirus, human metapneumovirus (hMPV), and respiratory syncytial virus; the other was tested using the FilmArray Respiratory Panel (bioMérieux). Specimens positive by either method underwent confirmatory quantitative real-time PCR to determine viral load. Sensitivity was stratified by viral load. A total of 1,584 paired specimens from 1,232 children (median age: 3.0 years [IQR: 1.0–6.0]; 53.7% male) were analyzed. Sensitivity of the antigen tests ranged from 20.6% (adenovirus) to 79.7% (hMPV), while specificity exceeded 99% for all six targets and overall agreement ranged from 90.7% to 99.0%. For every virus, antigen test positivity increased steeply with viral load, approaching 90–100% at viral loads ≥10 6 –10 7 copies/100 μL and falling below 50% at loads ≤10 4 –10 5 copies/100 μL. Antigen-based rapid tests for common pediatric respiratory viruses showed high specificity and viral-load-dependent sensitivity, detecting nearly all specimens with high viral load regardless of the target virus. These findings support a role for antigen testing in identifying children with the highest viral burden—who are most likely to have acute infection. IMPORTANCE The sensitivity of rapid antigen tests for respiratory viruses relative to PCR-based testing has been incompletely characterized. This study evaluated antigen tests for six common pediatric respiratory viruses—SARS-CoV-2, influenza A, influenza B, adenovirus, human metapneumovirus, and respiratory syncytial virus—against a multiplex PCR reference standard across 1,584 clinical specimens and linked test performance directly to quantitative viral load. We show that antigen test sensitivity is strongly and consistently dependent on viral load, approaching 90–100% at high viral loads with very high specificity across all six targets. These findings clarify the clinical role of rapid antigen testing: it reliably identifies children with the highest viral burden, who are most likely to have acute, symptomatic infection warranting immediate clinical action.

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在表征呼吸道病毒快速抗原检测的敏感性如何受到病毒载量的影响,特别是 人偏肺病毒 (hMPV)。这些测试相对于基于 PCR 的测试的敏感性尚未完全表征。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 这项前瞻性配对样本研究是在儿科中心进行的,从患有呼吸道感染 (RTI) 的儿童身上同时采集了两份鼻咽拭子。总共分析了来自 1,232 名儿童(中位年龄:3.0 岁 [IQR:1.0–6.0];53.7% 男性)的 1,584 个配对样本。
analysis_zh.methods: 对基于抗原的快速检测试剂盒或多重 PCR 检测呈阳性的样本进行验证性定量实时 PCR 以确定病毒载量。该研究针对 1,584 个临床样本的多重 PCR 参考标准,评估了六种常见儿科呼吸道病毒(包括 hMPV)的抗原测试。
analysis_zh.main_results: 抗原测试的敏感性范围为 20.6%(腺病毒)至 79.7%(hMPV),而所有六个目标的特异性均超过 99%,总体一致性范围为 90.7% 至 99.0%。对于每种病毒,抗原检测阳性率随着病毒载量的增加而急剧增加,在病毒载量≥10^6–10^7拷贝/100μL时接近90–100%,在病毒载量≤10^4–10^5拷贝/100μL时下降到50%以下。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果阐明了快速抗原检测的临床作用,表明它可以可靠地识别病毒负荷最高的儿童,这些儿童最有可能患有急性症状感染,需要立即采取临床行动。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现支持使用抗原检测来识别 hMPV 病毒载量较高的儿童,这可以为临床决策提供信息,并优先考虑对患有急性症状感染的儿童进行干预。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究的证据基于单一中心,可能无法推广到其他人群。证据强度中等,因为结果是基于特征明确的配对样本设计,与病毒载量有明确的联系。

papers.title: The MSC–RSV/HMPV interface: impacts on pulmonary homeostasis, remodeling, and risk of non-atopic asthma and COPD
papers.abstract: Respiratory tract infections continue to represent a major cause of pediatric morbidity and mortality. Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) and Human Metapneumovirus (HMPV) are highlighted as key etiologic agents of bronchiolitis and pneumonia, particularly in children under two years old. Recurrent infections during the second year of life may be associated with significant histopathological damage and might also be a risk factor for developing chronic pulmonary diseases, such as non-atopic asthma. In adults, these viruses similarly elevate clinical burden on the elderly and individuals with Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD), causing the exacerbation of respiratory signals and symptoms and, consequently, promoting a chronic inflammatory response that modifies the lung tissue and disease progression. Tissue repair and the homeostasis recovery might be associated with the participation of Mesenchymal Stem Cells (MSCs), both lung resident and migratory MSCs, these cells are characterized by their plasticity and immunomodulatory capacity, which are relevant to restoring tissue homeostasis after injury. However, RSV and HMPV may also infect MSCs, raising the question that infected MSCs could lose immunomodulatory efficacy and plasticity, thereby affecting tissue renewal. This review aims to provide an overview of the effect of respiratory viral infections, their implications in the lung tissue damage and the possible participation of MSCs in the recovery of lung homeostasis by tissue repair and immune response modulation.
papers.journal: Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology

Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) and Human Metapneumovirus (HMPV) are highlighted as key etiologic agents of bronchiolitis and pneumonia, particularly in children under two years old. Recurrent infections during the second year of life may be associated with significant histopathological damage and might also be a risk factor for developing chronic pulmonary diseases, such as non-atopic asthma. In adults, these viruses similarly elevate clinical burden on the elderly and individuals with Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD), causing the exacerbation of respiratory signals and symptoms and, consequently, promoting a chronic inflammatory response that modifies the lung tissue and disease progression. Tissue repair and the homeostasis recovery might be associated with the participation of Mesenchymal Stem Cells (MSCs), both lung resident and migratory MSCs, these cells are characterized by their plasticity and immunomodulatory capacity, which are relevant to restoring tissue homeostasis after injury. However, RSV and HMPV may also infect MSCs, raising the question that infected MSCs could lose immunomodulatory efficacy and plasticity, thereby affecting tissue renewal. This review aims to provide an overview of the effect of respiratory viral infections, their implications in the lung tissue damage and the possible participation of MSCs in the recovery of lung homeostasis by tissue repair and immune response modulation.

analysis.scope_and_question: This review focuses on the impact of Human Metapneumovirus (HMPV) infection on pulmonary homeostasis, remodeling, and the risk of non-atopic asthma and COPD. It explores the role of Mesenchymal Stem Cells (MSCs) in tissue repair and immune response modulation following HMPV infection.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is a narrative synthesis of existing literature, with no explicit mention of systematic search methods, databases, or meta-analysis. It includes general background information on HMPV and its association with respiratory infections, particularly in children and adults.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: There is consensus that HMPV is a significant etiologic agent of respiratory tract infections, especially in children under two years old. Recurrent infections during the second year of life are associated with histopathological damage and may increase the risk of chronic pulmonary diseases like non-atopic asthma. In adults, HMPV exacerbates respiratory symptoms and contributes to chronic inflammation in individuals with COPD.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review highlights the potential for HMPV to infect MSCs, which may affect their immunomodulatory capacity and plasticity, thereby influencing tissue renewal. However, the evidence is limited and does not provide a clear consensus on the mechanisms or outcomes of this interaction. There is a lack of detailed studies on the long-term effects of HMPV on lung tissue and the specific role of MSCs in recovery.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Further research is needed to understand the molecular mechanisms by which HMPV affects MSC function and to explore the potential of MSC-based therapies in mitigating lung damage and chronic disease progression. Clinical studies should focus on the long-term outcomes of HMPV infections and their impact on respiratory health.

analysis.summary_en: This review examines the role of Human Metapneumovirus (HMPV) in respiratory tract infections and its potential impact on pulmonary homeostasis, remodeling, and the development of chronic diseases such as non-atopic asthma and COPD. It highlights the involvement of Mesenchymal Stem Cells (MSCs) in tissue repair and immune response modulation following HMPV infection. While there is agreement on the clinical burden of HMPV, particularly in children and adults with COPD, the evidence is limited regarding the specific effects of HMPV on MSCs and the long-term consequences of infection. The review suggests that future research should focus on elucidating the mechanisms of MSC interaction with HMPV and the potential for MSC-based interventions in managing respiratory diseases.

papers.title: Respiratory Pathogens Detected among Pediatric Hospitalizations for Pneumonia: A Multicenter Study from Saitama, Japan.
papers.abstract: Routine in-hospital testing may not detect the full range of respiratory pathogens in children hospitalized with pneumonia. We conducted a prefecture-wide multicenter retrospective cohort study at four hospitals in Saitama, Japan, from July 2023 to March 2024 to describe detected respiratory pathogens and assess the additional findings obtained by multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR) beyond routine in-hospital testing. Among 1,170 pediatric hospitalizations for acute respiratory infections (ARIs), 457 (39.1%) were complicated by pneumonia. Human metapneumovirus (hMPV; n=124, 27.1%) and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV; n=85, 18.6%) were the most frequently detected pathogens. Multiplex PCR was performed in 199 hospitalizations. Among 123 hospitalizations in which at least one in-hospital respiratory pathogen test was performed and all results were negative, multiplex PCR detected at least one pathogen in 85 (69.1%). In an exploratory unadjusted comparison excluding 16 group A Streptococcus-positive hospitalizations, antibiotic initiation was associated with older age, higher C-reactive protein levels, and absence of a positive in-hospital test. Among 210 antibiotic-treated hospitalizations without a positive in-hospital test, 110 underwent multiplex PCR and a viral pathogen was detected in 74/110 (67.3%). Multiplex PCR frequently identified pathogens after negative routine testing and broadened the detectable pathogen spectrum beyond targeted in-hospital tests.

papers.title: Emerging Trends in the Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Management of Human Metapneumovirus-Associated Respiratory Infections
papers.abstract: Introduction: Human Metapneumovirus is a significant respiratory pathogen causing infections across all age groups, particularly in young children, immunocompromised individuals, and the elderly. Despite its clinical relevance, there are currently no approved vaccines or specific antiviral treatments for Human Metapneumovirus, necessitating further research into therapeutic and preventive strategies. Methods: A systematic literature review was conducted using peer-reviewed journals, clinical trials, and recent studies focusing on Human Metapneumovirus infection. Data were extracted and analyzed to evaluate the effectiveness of antiviral therapies, monoclonal antibodies, immunomodulators, and vaccine candidates. Results: Studies indicate that Human Metapneumovirus primarily targets the respiratory epithelium, triggering immune responses that contribute to both viral clearance and disease pathogenesis. Investigational therapies, including fusion inhibitors and protease inhibitors, show promise but require further validation. Immunomodulatory agents and herbal remedies may offer supportive benefits, but their efficacy against Human Metapneumovirus remains unproven. Advances in vaccine development are ongoing, with several candidates in preclinical and early clinical stages. Discussion: HMPV continues to pose a substantial public health burden due to its seasonal outbreaks, clinical similarity to other respiratory viruses, and absence of specific therapies. The virus evades immune responses via multiple mechanisms, contributing to disease severity, particularly in vulnerable populations. Although supportive care is currently the mainstay, emerging antivirals and vaccines may offer future solutions. Improved diagnostic access, public awareness, and targeted research are essential for controlling HMPV infections. Conclusion: Human Metapneumovirus continues to pose a public health challenge due to the lack of targeted treatments and vaccines. Ongoing research into antiviral agents, monoclonal antibodies, and vaccines is critical for effective disease management. Further clinical trials are needed to establish safe and effective therapeutic options.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores the pathogenesis, diagnosis, and management of human metapneumovirus (HMPV) infections, emphasizing its impact on vulnerable populations. The evidence highlights the virus's targeting of respiratory epithelium and the immune responses it triggers. While investigational therapies like fusion and protease inhibitors show promise, their efficacy remains unproven. Vaccine development is ongoing, with several candidates in early stages. The review underscores the need for further clinical trials, improved diagnostics, and public awareness to address the public health burden of HMPV. Despite the lack of specific treatments and vaccines, the study suggests that emerging antivirals and vaccines may offer future solutions.

elements_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 该病毒通过多种机制逃避 免疫应答,导致疾病严重化,特别是在弱势群体中。尽管目前支持性护理是主流,但新兴的 抗病毒药物 和 疫苗 可能会提供未来的解决方案。改善诊断途径、公众意识和有针对性的研究对于控制 HMPV 感染至关重要。需要进一步的临床试验来建立安全有效的治疗方案。
elements_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 针对抗病毒药物、单克隆抗体及疫苗的持续研究对于有效疾病管理至关重要。

papers.abstract_zh: 引言:人偏肺病毒(HMPV)是一种重要的呼吸道病原体,可在不同年龄段人群中引发感染,尤其是在幼儿、免疫功能低下者及老年人中。尽管其具有重要的临床意义,但目前尚无获批的抗病毒药物或针对人偏肺病毒的特异性治疗方法,亟需进一步研究治疗和预防策略。方法:通过系统性文献综述,检索同行评议期刊、临床试验及近期研究,重点关注人偏肺病毒感染。提取并分析数据,以评估抗病毒药物、单克隆抗体、免疫调节剂及疫苗候选物的有效性。结果:研究表明,人偏肺病毒主要靶向呼吸道上皮细胞,触发免疫应答,这些免疫应答既有助于病毒清除,也会导致疾病发病机制。正在研发的治疗方法,包括融合抑制剂和蛋白酶抑制剂,显示出潜力,但仍需进一步验证。免疫调节剂和中草药可能提供支持性益处,但其对人偏肺病毒的有效性尚未得到证实。疫苗研发取得进展,多个候选疫苗已进入临床前及早期临床阶段。讨论:由于人偏肺病毒的季节性流行、与其他呼吸道病毒的临床相似性以及缺乏特异性治疗方法,该病毒继续对公共卫生构成重大负担。该病毒通过多种机制逃避免疫应答,导致疾病严重程度增加,尤其是在易感人群中。尽管目前主要采用支持性治疗,但新兴的抗病毒药物和疫苗可能为未来提供解决方案。改善诊断可及性、提高公众意识及开展针对性研究对于控制人偏肺病毒感染至关重要。结论:由于缺乏针对性治疗方法和疫苗,人偏肺病毒继续对公共卫生构成挑战。针对抗病毒药物、单克隆抗体及疫苗的持续研究对于有效疾病管理至关重要。亟需进一步临床试验以确立安全有效的治疗方案。

papers.title: Human Metapneumovirus Nucleoprotein Impairs Stress-Induced Mitophagy and Mitochondrial Quality Control
papers.abstract: Human metapneumovirus (HMPV) is an important respiratory pathogen for which specific antiviral therapies are currently unavailable, and the mechanisms by which HMPV regulates host mitochondrial homeostasis remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the role of HMPV nucleoprotein (N) in mitophagy regulation and mitochondrial quality control, with a focus on its association with selective autophagy-related factors. Using recombinant protein purification, surface plasmon resonance, co-immunoprecipitation, confocal microscopy, mitochondrial-targeted mitophagy reporter analysis, and immunoblotting, we examined the interaction between HMPV N and host autophagy-associated factors and evaluated its effects on mitophagy. We demonstrated that HMPV N interacts with TAX1BP1 and LC3, two key components of the selective autophagy machinery. HMPV N signals were spatially associated with mitochondrial regions, and HMPV N expression increased the spatial association of TAX1BP1-positive structures with mitochondria, while reducing the spatial association of LC3-positive structures with TOM20-positive mitochondria under stress conditions. Consistently, HMPV N expression reduced CCCP-induced mitochondrial delivery to acidic compartments and attenuated TOM20 degradation, while exerting limited effects on basal mitochondrial turnover. These findings identify HMPV N as a viral regulator of stress-induced mitophagy and suggest that its interactions with selective autophagy-associated factors contribute to altered mitochondrial homeostasis during infection.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the role of HMPV nucleoprotein (N) in mitophagy regulation and mitochondrial quality control. The research aims to understand how HMPV affects host mitochondrial homeostasis, a poorly characterized area. Using a range of molecular and cellular techniques, the study demonstrates that HMPV N interacts with TAX1BP1 and LC3, key components of the selective autophagy machinery. The results show that HMPV N expression increases the spatial association of TAX1BP1-positive structures with mitochondria while reducing the association of LC3-positive structures with TOM20-positive mitochondria under stress conditions. These findings suggest that HMPV N modulates stress-induced mitophagy through interactions with autophagy-related factors, potentially contributing to altered mitochondrial homeostasis during infection. The study provides insights into the molecular mechanisms of HMPV pathogenesis, which could inform future research on antiviral strategies and mitochondrial-targeted therapies. However, the study is limited to in vitro and cell-based experiments, which may not fully represent in vivo conditions. The evidence is strong based on the experimental methods and results, but further studies are needed to validate these findings in clinical settings.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 人偏肺病毒 (HMPV) 是一种重要的呼吸道病原体,目前尚无特定的 抗病毒药物 疗法,并且 HMPV 调节 宿主 线粒体稳态的机制仍知之甚少。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 在这里,我们研究了 HMPV 核蛋白 (N) 在线粒体自噬调节和线粒体质量控制中的作用,重点关注其与选择性自噬相关因子的关联。
elements_zh.methods: 利用重组蛋白纯化、表面等离子共振、免疫共沉淀、共聚焦显微镜、线粒体靶向线粒体自噬报告基因分析和免疫印迹,我们检测了 HMPV N 和 宿主 自噬相关因子之间的相互作用,并评估了其对线粒体自噬的影响。
elements_zh.main_results: 我们证明了 HMPV N 与选择性自噬机制的两个关键组成部分 TAX1BP1 和 LC3 相互作用。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: HMPV N 信号与线粒体区域在空间上相关,并且在应激条件下,HMPV N 表达增加了 TAX1BP1 阳性结构与线粒体的空间关联,同时减少了 LC3 阳性结构与 TOM20 阳性线粒体的空间关联。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 一致地,HMPV N 表达减少了 CCCP 诱导的线粒体向酸性区室的递送并减弱了 TOM20 降解,同时对基础线粒体周转产生有限的影响。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 这些发现将 HMPV N 确定为应激诱导线粒体自噬的病毒调节剂,并表明其与选择性自噬相关因子的相互作用有助于改变感染期间的线粒体稳态。

papers.full_text: SummaryCoinfections may influence the clinical outcome of respiratory illness. Data are limited regarding RSV coinfections in adults with high‐risk conditions. Residual respiratory specimens from community‐dwelling adults (≥ 18 years) with ≥ 1 high‐risk condition were retested using a multiplex panel for multiple viral pathogens. We compared demographic and clinical characteristics between those with RSV coinfection versus RSV single infection. RSV coinfections comprised 5.9% of all RSV infections among adults with ≥ 1 high‐risk condition. No statistically significant differences were observed between those with RSV coinfections and single infections according to presence of specific high‐risk conditions or clinical disease presentation.Keywords: adults, coinfections, high‐risk conditions, respiratory syncytial virus 2.MethodsThis retrospective cohort study used existing data and archived respiratory specimens from community‐dwelling adult participants who were originally enrolled in test‐negative studies of influenza vaccine effectiveness (VE) during 2015–2020 winter seasons. The details of these VE studies have been described in detail elsewhere [4] and are summarized briefly below.2.1.Influenza Vaccine Effectiveness StudyOriginal VE studies enrolled Marshfield Clinic Health System (MCHS) patients in Marshfield, WI, concordant with an outpatient clinic encounter for an acute respiratory illness (ARI), during winter seasons (January 2016–April 2016, January 2017–April 2017, December 2017–April 2018, January 2019–April 2019, December 2019–March 2020). Eligible participants had illness duration of ≤ 7 days at the time of enrollment. Individuals with enrollment in the past 14 days or receipt of an antiviral drug before sample collection were ineligible. Participants provided respiratory samples (nasal and throat) for influenza testing. Residual samples were subsequently archived.2.2.Current StudyThe current analysis included VE study participants aged ≥ 18 years with ≥ 1 high‐risk condition. Archived respiratory samples were retested on a multiplex panel (GenMark ePlex Respiratory Pathogen Panel) [5] for adenovirus (AdV), seasonal coronaviruses (CoV; types 229E, HKU1, NL63, OC43), human metapneumovirus (hMPV), rhinovirus/enterovirus (RV), influenza virus (IFV; A/H1, A/H1pdm09, H3, B), parainfluenza virus (PIV; types 1–4), and RSV (types A, B). RSV coinfection was defined as detection of ≥ 2 viral pathogens, one of which was RSV A or B and the other non‐RSV. Infection with RSV A and B simultaneously, without the presence of a non‐RSV pathogen, was not considered a coinfection. High‐risk conditions were defined using International Classification of Diseases (ICD) codes documented in the electronic health record (EHR) (Appendix A). Conditions were grouped into cardiac disorders, chronic respiratory diseases, chronic liver disease, chronic kidney disease, diabetes, and immunocompromised status. Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) score at time of VE study enrollment, and hospitalization within 30 days of enrollment visit, were also obtained from the EHR.2.3.Ethics StatementThe MCHS institutional review board reviewed and approved this study with a waiver of informed consent. Patients provided consent before participating in the original Flu VE study. 4.ResultsOf 3601 samples retested from eligible enrollments of high‐risk adults, RSV was detected in 303 (8.4%). Among RSV‐positive samples, 39.6% were from adults aged ≥ 65 years, 65.7% from females, and 69.6% from those who received influenza vaccine in the past year (Table 1).Table 1Demographic and clinical For example, it is possible for an individual to have both a cardiac disorder and an immunocompromising condition. h Cardiac disorders include arrhythmias, heart failure, and coronary artery disease. i Chronic respiratory diseases include COPD, asthma, and cystic fibrosis. j Immunocompromising conditions include individuals with transplants (not restricted to solid organ transplant), malignancies, immunosuppressive therapy, and/or other immunodeficiencies.Among RSV‐positive samples, 18 (5.9%) were coinfections and 285 (94.1%) were single infections. Prevalence of RSV coinfections varied by age, and occurred with RV (n = 8; 44.4%); IFV (n = 6; 33.3%); CoV (n = 5; 27.8%); and AdV (n = 1; 5.6%) (Figure 1). Demographic characteristics and high‐risk conditions among those with RSV single versus coinfections are shown in Table 1.Figure 1Distribution of RSV viral‐viral coinfections by number of respiratory samples tested. *Two respiratory samples were positive for RSV + HRV/HEV + IFV. AdV, adenovirus; CoV, coronaviruses (seasonal); EV, enterovirus; HMpV, human metapneumovirus; IFV, influenza virus; PIV, parainfluenza virus; RSV, respiratory syncytial virus. RV, rhinovirusIn the 30 days after enrollment, there were 0 hospitalizations among RSV coinfections and 8 hospitalizations (2.6%) among RSV single infections. During this period, RSV‐coinfected individuals experienced 2 (11.1%), 1 (5.6%) and 1 (5.6%) cases of asthma exacerbation, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exacerbation, and pneumonia, respectively. Among RSV single infections, there were 10 (3.5%), 19 (6.7%) and 13 (4.6%) cases with asthma exacerbation, COPD exacerbation, and pneumonia, respectively. There were no statistically significant differences between those with RSV coinfections versus single infections by age group, sex, vaccination status, presence of upper or lower respiratory symptoms, or high‐risk conditions. 5.DiscussionIn this retrospective cohort study of high‐risk adults, RSV coinfections comprised 5.9% of all RSV outpatient ARI. The relatively low proportion of RSV coinfections observed among high‐risk adults in our study is consistent with previous studies of hospitalized children and adults, where respiratory viral coinfections (including coinfections with RSV) varied from 5.0% to 14.4%, and were inversely associated with age [6, 7]. RSV coinfection was most common with RV and IFV in our study, consistent with other studies that have reported higher proportions of RSV/RV in adult coinfections [8, 9].Existing literature has reported a higher proportion and incidence of RSV infections versus no infection in adults with cardiac disorders compared to other comorbidities, as well as increased morbidity and mortality due to RSV infections in general among adults with underlying COPD or congestive heart failure (CHF) compared to adults without comorbidities [10, 11, 12]. We identified no statistically significant differences between RSV coinfections and RSV single infections according to high‐risk conditions, potentially as a result of limited statistical power.Our study had several limitations. This analysis had a relatively small sample size and low number of RSV coinfections detected, limiting our ability to detect differences in coinfection and single‐infection groups. Additionally, we were limited in our ability to detect coinfections by the pathogens present in the multiplex panel, though the panel included common viral respiratory pathogens. Our study period was before the COVID‐19 pandemic, and does not include coinfections with RSV and SARS‐CoV‐2. Furthermore, our analysis is limited to ARI identified in the outpatient setting. As such, it necessarily excludes high‐risk patients who sought care only in the hospital or emergency department. This limits generalizability of our findings. Although our identification of high‐risk conditions is in keeping with other studies on RSV in adults, there is likely to be heterogeneity in severity of comorbid conditions within high‐risk groups. Many epidemiological assessments of RSV in high‐risk adults have focused on hospitalized cohorts and report clinical outcomes of severe illness, such as hospitalization, ICU admission, and death [11, 13]. Finally, our study population was predominantly non‐Hispanic White, which may limit the generalizability of study findings.In a multiseason study of high‐risk adults with ARI, we found that RSV coinfections are relatively uncommon in the outpatient setting, and do not differ significantly from RSV single infection by high‐risk conditions or disease presentation. RSV coinfections in children are associated with increased disease severity, including pneumonia, severe bronchiolitis, and hospitalization [3]. However, there are limited data on the significance of RSV coinfections in adults with high‐risk conditions (“high‐risk adults”), who may be at increased risk for severe infection. Eligible participants had illness duration of ≤ 7 days at the time of enrollment. Individuals with enrollment in the past 14 days or receipt of an antiviral drug before sample collection were ineligible. Participants provided respiratory samples (nasal and throat) for influenza testing. Residual samples were subsequently archived. 2.2.Current StudyThe current analysis included VE study participants aged ≥ 18 years with ≥ 1 high‐risk condition. Archived respiratory samples were retested on a multiplex panel (GenMark ePlex Respiratory Pathogen Panel) [5] for adenovirus (AdV), seasonal coronaviruses (CoV; types 229E, HKU1, NL63, OC43), human metapneumovirus (hMPV), rhinovirus/enterovirus (RV), influenza virus (IFV; A/H1, A/H1pdm09, H3, B), parainfluenza virus (PIV; types 1–4), and RSV (types A, B). RSV coinfection was defined as detection of ≥ 2 viral pathogens, one of which was RSV A or B and the other non‐RSV. Infection with RSV A and B simultaneously, without the presence of a non‐RSV pathogen, was not considered a coinfection. High‐risk conditions were defined using International Classification of Diseases (ICD) codes documented in the electronic health record (EHR) (Appendix A). Conditions were grouped into cardiac disorders, chronic respiratory diseases, chronic liver disease, chronic kidney disease, diabetes, and immunocompromised status. Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) score at time of VE study enrollment, and hospitalization within 30 days of enrollment visit, were also obtained from the EHR. 2.3.Ethics StatementThe MCHS institutional review board reviewed and approved this study with a waiver of informed consent. Patients provided consent before participating in the original Flu VE study. 3.Statistical AnalysisThe prevalence of RSV coinfection was calculated as the proportion of enrollments with RSV A or B and ≥ 1 non‐RSV pathogen(s), among total RSV‐positive enrollments. Prevalence of RSV single infection was calculated as the proportion of enrollments with RSV A or B only, among total RSV‐positive enrollments. Differences in demographic and clinical characteristics between RSV coinfections versus single infections were assessed using two‐tailed chi‐square, Fisher's exact, or Wilcoxon rank‐sum tests, as appropriate. Absolute differences in proportions and Wald 95% confidence intervals (CIs) between groups were calculated; p < 0.05 were considered statistically significant. Analyses were performed using Stata v19 (College Station, TX) and SAS v9.4 (Cary, NC). Multivariable analyses were not conducted due to sparse analytic strata. full_text_sections.discussion: 5.DiscussionIn this retrospective cohort study of high‐risk adults, RSV coinfections comprised 5.9% of all RSV outpatient ARI. The relatively low proportion of RSV coinfections observed among high‐risk adults in our study is consistent with previous studies of hospitalized children and adults, where respiratory viral coinfections (including coinfections with RSV) varied from 5.0% to 14.4%, and were inversely associated with age [6, 7]. RSV coinfection was most common with RV and IFV in our study, consistent with other studies that have reported higher proportions of RSV/RV in adult coinfections [8, 9].Existing literature has reported a higher proportion and incidence of RSV infections versus no infection in adults with cardiac disorders compared to other comorbidities, as well as increased morbidity and mortality due to RSV infections in general among adults with underlying COPD or congestive heart failure (CHF) compared to adults without comorbidities [10, 11, 12]. We identified no statistically significant differences between RSV coinfections and RSV single infections according to high‐risk conditions, potentially as a result of limited statistical power.Our study had several limitations. This analysis had a relatively small sample size and low number of RSV coinfections detected, limiting our ability to detect differences in coinfection and single‐infection groups. Additionally, we were limited in our ability to detect coinfections by the pathogens present in the multiplex panel, though the panel included common viral respiratory pathogens. Our study period was before the COVID‐19 pandemic, and does not include coinfections with RSV and SARS‐CoV‐2. Furthermore, our analysis is limited to ARI identified in the outpatient setting. As such, it necessarily excludes high‐risk patients who sought care only in the hospital or emergency department. This limits generalizability of our findings. Although our identification of high‐risk conditions is in keeping with other studies on RSV in adults, there is likely to be heterogeneity in severity of comorbid conditions within high‐risk groups. Many epidemiological assessments of RSV in high‐risk adults have focused on hospitalized cohorts and report clinical outcomes of severe illness, such as hospitalization, ICU admission, and death [11, 13]. Finally, our study population was predominantly non‐Hispanic White, which may limit the generalizability of study findings.In a multiseason study of high‐risk adults with ARI, we found that RSV coinfections are relatively uncommon in the outpatient setting, and do not differ significantly from RSV single infection by high‐risk conditions or disease presentation. There is a need for ongoing research to assess the burden of RSV coinfections in adults with high‐risk conditions who are most likely to benefit from RSV vaccination.
full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionCoinfections with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and other respiratory pathogens may affect symptoms and disease severity [1, 2]. RSV coinfections in children are associated with increased disease severity, including pneumonia, severe bronchiolitis, and hospitalization [3]. However, there are limited data on the significance of RSV coinfections in adults with high‐risk conditions (“high‐risk adults”), who may be at increased risk for severe infection. We identified RSV coinfections among high‐risk adults during five winter seasons, and compared demographic and clinical characteristics between those with RSV coinfections versus single infections. 2.1.Influenza Vaccine Effectiveness StudyOriginal VE studies enrolled Marshfield Clinic Health System (MCHS) patients in Marshfield, WI, concordant with an outpatient clinic encounter for an acute respiratory illness (ARI), during winter seasons (January 2016–April 2016, January 2017–April 2017, December 2017–April 2018, January 2019–April 2019, December 2019–March 2020). Eligible participants had illness duration of ≤ 7 days at the time of enrollment. Individuals with enrollment in the past 14 days or receipt of an antiviral drug before sample collection were ineligible. Participants provided respiratory samples (nasal and throat) for influenza testing. Residual samples were subsequently archived. 2.2.Current StudyThe current analysis included VE study participants aged ≥ 18 years with ≥ 1 high‐risk condition. Archived respiratory samples were retested on a multiplex panel (GenMark ePlex Respiratory Pathogen Panel) [5] for adenovirus (AdV), seasonal coronaviruses (CoV; types 229E, HKU1, NL63, OC43), human metapneumovirus (hMPV), rhinovirus/enterovirus (RV), influenza virus (IFV; A/H1, A/H1pdm09, H3, B), parainfluenza virus (PIV; types 1–4), and RSV (types A, B). RSV coinfection was defined as detection of ≥ 2 viral pathogens, one of which was RSV A or B and the other non‐RSV. Infection with RSV A and B simultaneously, without the presence of a non‐RSV pathogen, was not considered a coinfection. High‐risk conditions were defined using International Classification of Diseases (ICD) codes documented in the electronic health record (EHR) (Appendix A). Conditions were grouped into cardiac disorders, chronic respiratory diseases, chronic liver disease, chronic kidney disease, diabetes, and immunocompromised status. Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) score at time of VE study enrollment, and hospitalization within 30 days of enrollment visit, were also obtained from the EHR. 2.3.Ethics StatementThe MCHS institutional review board reviewed and approved this study with a waiver of informed consent. Patients provided consent before participating in the original Flu VE study. 3.Statistical AnalysisThe prevalence of RSV coinfection was calculated as the proportion of enrollments with RSV A or B and ≥ 1 non‐RSV pathogen(s), among total RSV‐positive enrollments. Prevalence of RSV single infection was calculated as the proportion of enrollments with RSV A or B only, among total RSV‐positive enrollments. Differences in demographic and clinical characteristics between RSV coinfections versus single infections were assessed using two‐tailed chi‐square, Fisher's exact, or Wilcoxon rank‐sum tests, as appropriate. Absolute differences in proportions and Wald 95% confidence intervals (CIs) between groups were calculated; p < 0.05 were considered statistically significant. Analyses were performed using Stata v19 (College Station, TX) and SAS v9.4 (Cary, NC). Multivariable analyses were not conducted due to sparse analytic strata. analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate RSV coinfections in high-risk adults, addressing a knowledge gap regarding the significance of RSV coinfections in this population, which may be at increased risk for severe infection.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective observational study of 3601 respiratory samples from adults with high-risk conditions over five winter seasons from 2015 to 2020, focusing on RSV coinfections.
analysis.methods: Residual respiratory specimens from community-dwelling adults with ≥1 high-risk conditions were retested using a multiplex panel for multiple viral pathogens, with RSV coinfection defined as detection of ≥2 viral pathogens, one of which was RSV A or B and the other non-RSV.
analysis.main_results: RSV was detected in 303 (8.4%) of 3601 samples, with 5.9% of RSV-positive adults having coinfections, primarily with rhinovirus (RV) and influenza virus (IFV).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study found that RSV coinfections were most common with RV and IFV, and there were no statistically significant differences between coinfections and single infections according to high-risk conditions, potentially due to limited statistical power.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that RSV coinfections may be associated with increased disease severity in high-risk adults, highlighting the need for further research and surveillance in this population.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study had a relatively small sample size and low number of RSV coinfections detected, limiting the ability to detect differences between coinfections and single infections. The study period was before the COVID-19 pandemic and did not include coinfections with SARS-CoV-2.

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在调查高危成人中 RSV 合并感染的情况,解决该人群中 RSV 合并感染重要性的知识差距,因为该人群严重感染的风险可能会增加。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 对 2015 年至 2020 年五个冬季的 3601 份高危成年人呼吸道样本进行回顾性观察研究,重点关注 RSV 合并感染。
analysis_zh.methods: 使用多重检测组对患有 ≥1 种高危病症的社区居住成年人的残留呼吸道标本进行了多种病毒病原体的重新检测,RSV 合并感染定义为检测到 ≥2 种病毒病原体,其中一种是 RSV A 或 B,另一种是非 RSV。
analysis_zh.main_results: 3601 份样本中的 303 份(8.4%)检测到 RSV,其中 5.9% 的 RSV 阳性成年人同时感染,主要是鼻病毒 (RV) 和流感病毒 (IFV)。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究发现,RSV 合并感染以 RV 和 IFV 最为常见,并且根据高危情况,合并感染与单一感染之间没有统计学上的显着差异,这可能是由于统计功效有限。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,RSV 合并感染可能与高危成人疾病严重程度增加有关,这凸显了对该人群进行进一步研究和 监测 的必要性。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究的样本量相对较小,检测到的 RSV 合并感染数量也较少,限制了检测合并感染和单一感染之间差异的能力。研究时期是在 COVID-19 大流行之前,不包括与 SARS-CoV-2 的合并感染。

papers.full_text: BackgroundTo date, accessible diagnostic tools to identify whether a patient's pneumonia is a bacterial, or viral infection, are not accurate or timely enough to prevent preemptive antibiotic administration. Relying on single biomarkers or clinical presentations has been insufficient. We aimed to incorporate a wide range of novel biomarkers and clinical presentations into a multivariable model and to validate its ability to differentiate bacterial from viral pneumonia.MethodsA total of 457 children aged 2–59 months, admitted to the Kilifi County Referral Hospital, Kenya, with WHO defined pneumonia were classified using gold standard laboratory diagnostics as possible bacterial (i.e., bacterial/ unknown cases, n = 229) or possible viral (n = 228) infections. Clinical and laboratory data, and levels of CRP, PCT and 6 novel protein biomarkers were used to develop and validate a predictive multivariable Poisson regression model to differentiate pneumonia etiology. The Receiver Operating Characteristic curve was used to assess biomarker performance and validate the model internally.ResultsIn age-adjusted analyses, chest-wall indrawing, cough, convulsions, crackles, angiotensinogen (AGT), and Serpin Family A Member 1 (SERPINA1) were significantly associated with pneumonia etiology, controlling for age. However, only chest-wall indrawing remained significant in multivariable analyses after controlling for age. The model demonstrated fair, but inadequate, discrimination, with an Area Under the Curve of 0.61. In a separate analysis excluding the unknowns from the bacterial group, chest-wall indrawing, crackles, cough, AGT (>=7.9144MFI), were significant predictors of pneumonia etiology, adjusting for age. This model demonstrated good discrimination, with an Area Under the Curve of 0.78 on the validation dataset.ConclusionAmong children admitted to the hospital with WHO-defined pneumonia, modelling a wide range of biomarkers and clinical presentations still failed to distinguish bacterial from viral pneumonia with enough accuracy to guide clinical management. Further research addressing some of the limitations we encountered in outcome classification, stratifying by disease severity and potentially accounting for variation in biomarker performance by age, may improve predictions. Materials and methodsStudy setting and populationData on children presenting to Kilifi County Referral Hospital (KCRH) with pneumonia were derived from the long-term surveillance of Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) in childhood lower respiratory tract infection study, conducted between January 2007 and August 2020. This project sampled children less than 5 years of age who were either febrile or presented with sepsis or pneumonia for biomarker discovery and validation (8). Children were excluded if born prematurely, were less than 1 week of age, or had a history of congenital heart disease. For the analysis presented here, this nested case-control study selected data from children aged 2–59 months who met the 2013 WHO definition of pneumonia (22). This study utilized secondary data, and therefore, the patients were participants in the study and were not involved in the design, conduct, or dissemination plan of this study's findings.Study proceduresUnder the surveillance protocol, anthropometric (e.g., weight, height), clinical (e.g., cough, cyanosis, hypoxemia), and demographic data (e.g., age, gender), blood samples, and nasopharyngeal/oropharyngeal (NP/OP) swabs were collected at admission. NP/OP swabs were used to test for 15 common childhood viral infections, including adenovirus, parainfluenza virus (1,2,3, and 4), RSV (A and B), influenza (A, B, and C), rhinovirus, human metapneumovirus, and coronaviruses (OC43, NL63, and E229) using multiplex real-time PCR. Blood specimens were cultured for bacteria, and a blood slide was prepared to determine malaria infection status. Blood samples were analyzed with a complete blood count [WBC, red blood cell counts (RBC), platelets, neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils]. The biomarker discovery study tested the blood samples from a subset of children and quantified 418 plasma proteins using high-performance liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (HPLC-MS/MS) [11]. CRP and 6 other plasma proteins appeared predictive of infectious aetiology: angiotensinogen (AGT), Serpin Family A Member 1 (SERPINA1), Serpin Family A Member 3 (SERPINA3), Paraoxonase-1 (PON1), Histidine Rich Glycoprotein (HRG/B2R8I2), and lipopolysaccharide-binding protein (LBP) [11] and were therefore considered for etiology differentiation for this study. Samples from the whole cohort of children were then tested for CRP, PCT, and these 6 novel proteins using the same mass spectrometry. The ILab Aries clinical biochemistry analyzer was used to measure a subset of 100 CRP samples, which were converted to concentrations (8). Laboratory sample testing was conducted at the KEMRI-Wellcome Trust Research Programme (KWTRP) in Kilifi, Kenya.Statistical analysesFor the secondary data analysis presented in this paper, pneumonia cases were classified as viral, bacterial, bacterial-viral co-infections, and unknown infections (Figure 1). For clinical relevance, we combined children with evidence of bacterial infections, bacterial-viral co-infections, and unknown infections into a single group (possible bacterial infections) that would need to receive empirical antibiotic therapy if presenting to a healthcare facility. Children whose NP/OP swabs were PCR + for viral infections known to cause pneumonia [adenovirus, parainfluenza virus (1,2,3, and 4), RSV (A and B), influenza (A, B, and C), and human metapneumovirus] were defined as the probable viral pneumonia group.Figure 1This is the participants’ flowchart. It provides a detailed explanation of the flow by which the study determined the working sample size. It also shows which criteria of participants were eliminated and the pathogens that guided our case definition.Flowchart illustrating sample selection for a study on severe acute infections in children, detailing initial enrollment, exclusion criteria, final classification into bacterial and viral groups, and splitting of the dataset into training and testing sets.Variables such as cough duration were missing in >25% of participants and excluded from the analysis. Using the training dataset, excluding children with infections of unknown aetiology and bacterial-viral co-infections, the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve was used to identify optimal cutoff points for the mean fluorescent intensity (MFI) values of biomarkers, enabling categorization into categorical variables with the highest sensitivity, specificity, and overall discriminatory ability. The cutpointr package in R was utilized to determine the optimal threshold of each biomarker using the Youden index (sensitivity + specificity – 1). To enhance the robustness of the estimates, a 5-fold cross-validation stratified by etiology was used to assess the discriminatory power of each candidate biomarker and to identify the optimal threshold (cut-offs). These derived cut-offs from the training set were then applied unchanged to the validation dataset. Further exploratory analyses to determine cut-off points for biomarkers were also identified by stratifying the dataset by age (<1 and ≥1 years, <2 and ≥2 years, and <3 and ≥3 years) on the entire dataset to assess whether cut-offs varied by age, as this has been reported in some previous literature (26). The Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) was used to evaluate multicollinearity among variables. Highly correlated variables (VIF >2) were assessed for their discriminatory power. The variable with the lower AUC was dropped. Exploratory interaction analyses were conducted after the primary analyses to assess whether an interaction between pneumonia severity and the eight biomarkers, adjusting for age, could explain the biomarkers’ performance. Interaction terms were included in separate modified Poisson regression models and significance assessed using the Wald test with robust standard errors.Model developmentThe dataset was randomly split into two datasets, stratified by etiology; 70% of the data was used for training and 30% for model validation. Age was considered a priori as a confounder in every stage of the analysis. A modified Poisson regression model was used to assess the association between every predictor and the outcome. Covariates with a likelihood ratio test (LRT) p-value < 0.2 in the age-adjusted analyses were considered to improve model fit and were therefore included in the selection for the multivariable predictive model. The multivariable Poisson regression model was fitted using backward selection. Variables were iteratively removed from the multivariate model, and variables that significantly improved the model's fit (LRT p-value < 0.05) were retained in the final model. The overall sensitivity, specificity, and discriminative power (AUC) of the final model for distinguishing bacterial from viral pneumonia cases were assessed. To assess the stability of the model development process and performance, a 5-fold cross-validation, stratified by etiology, on the training set was performed. Within each fold, 4 folds were used as the model development sets, while one fold was held out for out-of-sample model validation. The complete model-building procedure was performed in each fold, adjusting for age. First, each predictor was assessed for its association with etiology, using an LRT p-value <0.2 to identify potential predictors for inclusion in the multivariable model. Backward elimination was then performed, and variables with an LRT p-value <0.05 were retained in the multivariable models. The models’ performance was then assessed on the out-of-sample validation dataset using the AUC. The overall model performance was recorded as the mean AUC of the 5 cross-validation folds.Model validationThe model's ability to distinguish between bacterial and viral pneumonia cases was assessed using Area Under the Curve (AUC) values on the validation dataset. Other published predictive models were also run on the validation dataset to determine comparative discriminatory power. An AUC of 0.5 indicated that the model cannot discriminate beyond chance; a value greater than 0.7 was considered moderate discrimination, while a value greater than 0.80 was regarded as good discrimination (23). The model's calibration was assessed using the calibration intercept, which measures how close the predicted risks are to the observed event (underestimation or overestimation), and the calibration slope, which indicates potential model overfit or underfit (23). We externally validated a previously published model (15), developed in a study of Indonesian children aged 2–59 months with pneumonia (WHO 2014 definition) who were hospitalised within 24 h of admission, by applying their logistic regression model to our dataset without modification. We defined the variables in their final model as in their publication, without refitting or recalibrating it. Another study (9) conducted in Western Australian children ≤17 years of age recommended a CRP cutoff of 72 mg/L in the presence of fever (≥38 °C) or absence of rhinorrhea. We validated these models using CRP data analysed on the ILab Aries clinical biochemistry analyser. All statistical analyses were conducted using R software version 4.5.1, and variable significance was evaluated at a 5% significance level.Ethics approvalThe long-term surveillance of RSV in childhood lower respiratory tract infections study (SSC 1055) was approved by the Kenya Medical Research Institute Scientific Ethics Research Unit (KEMRI–SERU) and conducted in accordance with the principles of Good Clinical Practice and Good Clinical Laboratory Practice (GCLP). Written informed consent was obtained from the participant's respective legal guardian or next of kin, and the study adhered to the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki. For this nested study, data were shared with the approval of the study Principal Investigator and the KWTRP data governance committee. ResultsAmong the 457 children enrolled in this study, 228 (49.9%) had NP/OP swabs PCR + for viral infections known to cause pneumonia and no evidence of other infections, 93 (20.4%) had a positive blood culture for a bacterial infection, 12 (2.6%) had a bacterial-viral co-infection, and 124 (27.1%) had unknown etiology (i.e., negative blood culture, negative PCR panel, negative malaria slide; Figure 1). Among the 228 with a viral infection, the most identified viral pathogens were RSV-A (n = 39, 17.1%), parainfluenza-3 (n = 36, 15.8%), human metapneumovirus (n = 35, 15.4%), influenza-A (n = 34, 14.9%), and adenovirus (n = 28, 12.3%). The most identified bacterial pathogens from blood cultures were Escherichia coli (n = 17, 7.4%), Streptococcus pneumoniae (n = 17, 7.4%), Staphylococcus aureus (n = 11, 4.8%), and Haemophilus influenzae (n = 8, 3.5%). (Supplementary Figures S1, S2).Demographic, laboratory, and clinical characteristicsMore than half (63%) of the study population had severe pneumonia compared to (non-severe) pneumonia (37%) (Supplementary Table S2). A higher proportion of children with probable viral pneumonia presented with severe pneumonia (72%), compared to children with possible bacterial pneumonia (54%) (Supplementary Table S2). Cell counts of WBC (p-value = 0.002), neutrophils (p-value = 0.017), and the median fluorescent intensity (MFI) units of AGT (p-value = 0.002), LBP (p-value = 0.005), PCT (p-value = 0.020), and SERPINA1 (p-value = 0.002) were significantly higher in the bacterial group, while the cell counts of RBC (p-value = 0.014), hemoglobin (p-value = 0.029) concentrations, and MFI units of SERPINA3 (p-value = 0.014) were significantly higher in the viral group (Supplementary Table S1).Predictive capacity of each biomarker to differentiate bacterial from viral infectionsBased on this nested study's case definition, AGT had the best discriminatory power (AUC = 0.60, 95% CI [0.53, 0.66]), followed by PCT (AUC = 0.58, 95% CI [0.52, 0.64]) and SERPINA1 (AUC = 0.58, 95% CI [0.52, 0.64]), and lastly LBP (AUC = 0.56, 95% CI [0.50, 0.63] (Table 1)). CRP, HRG, PON1, and SERPINA3 could not distinguish bacterial from viral infections beyond chance as their confidence intervals had limits below 0.50 (Table S1). Assessing the biomarker performance on ‘pure’ bacterial and viral infections of pneumonia, AGT (AUC = 0.76, 95% CI [0.69, 0.83]) had the highest discriminatory power, followed by PCT (AUC = 0.65, 95% CI [0.57, 0.73]), LBP (AUC = 0.65, 95% CI [0.56, 0.73]), and SERPINA1 (AUC = 0.65, 95% CI [0.56, 0.73]) while SERPINA3 (AUC = 0.56, 95% CI [0.48, 0.65]) and HRG (AUC = 0.57, 95% CI [0.49, 0.65]) could not discriminate beyond chance (Supplementary Table S5). There was a high degree of overlap observed across the bacterial and viral biomarker levels (Figure 2). In assessing interactions between pneumonia severity and biomarkers, there was a significant interaction between pneumonia severity and AGT (RR = 0.85, p-value = 0.0080), CRP (RR = 0.77, p-value = 0.0073), HRG (RR = 0.85, p-value = 0.0380), and SERPINA1 (RR = 0.80, p-value = 0.0058) (Supplementary Table S8).Table 1Biomarker thresholds derived when comparing all possible bacterial cases and probable viral cases, and their sensitivity and specificity in differentiating between all possible bacterial cases and probable viral cases.BiomarkerThreshold (MFI)SensitivitySpecificityPPVNPVAUC [95% CI]AGT7.91440.490.720.640.580.60 [0.53, 0.66]CRP9.15140.900.190.530.660.54 [0.48, 0.61]PCT6.10210.240.900.710.820.58 [0.52, 0.64]LBP7.66170.330.840.680.780.56 [0.50, 0.63]HRG7.71320.640.460.540.620.53 [0.46, 0.59]PON15.97970.660.450.550.620.54 [0.48, 0.61]SERPINA18.97410.290.910.750.860.58 [0.52, 0.64]SERPINA38.74650.390.700.570.660.53 [0.47, 0.59]Area Under the Curve (AUC) represents the discriminatory power of each predictor in distinguishing bacterial from viral pneumonia. Sensitivity is the proportion of true bacterial cases accurately identified by each predictor. Specificity is the proportion of true viral cases accurately identified by each predictor. Positive Predictive Value (PPV) is the proportion of cases predicted as bacterial that are truly bacterial. Negative Predictive Value (NPV) is the proportion of cases predicted as viral that are truly not bacterial.Figure 2This is a density plot showing how the biomarker median fluorescent intensity (MFI) levels between the bacterial and viral groups of infection overlap.Seven density plots compare biomarker MFI values between viral (blue) and bacterial (red) infection for AGT, CRP, HRG, LBP, PCT, PON1, SERPINA1, and SERPINA3. X-axes display biomarker MFI value; y-axes show density. Distributions for each biomarker differ between virus and bacteria groups, as indicated by colored overlays. Aetiology legend is at right.Modified poisson regression analysesIn age-adjusted analyses, restricted to the training set, mid-upper arm circumference, chest-wall indrawing, cough, convulsion, crackles, AGT (in continuous and categorical forms), and SERPINA1 (in a categorical form that used different cut-offs for children <1 and ≥1 year of age) were predictive of pneumonia etiology (Table 2). In multivariable analyses controlling for age, only lower chest-wall indrawing (LCWI) (aRR = 0.75, 95% CI [0.61, 0.93], p-value = 0.0081) remained a significant predictor, with a higher prevalence in the viral pneumonia group. After controlling for age and LCWI, none of the other clinical signs or symptoms, or biomarker levels, was predictive of etiology (Table 2).Table 2Predictors of pneumonia etiology identified in the training dataset using a multivariable poisson regression model.CharacteristicOverallN = 319aProbable viralN = 159aPossible bacterialN = 160aCrude RR [95% CI]LRT p-valueAdjusted RR [95% CI]LR…

This study utilized secondary data, and therefore, the patients were participants in the study and were not involved in the design, conduct, or dissemination plan of this study's findings.Study proceduresUnder the surveillance protocol, anthropometric (e.g., weight, height), clinical (e.g., cough, cyanosis, hypoxemia), and demographic data (e.g., age, gender), blood samples, and nasopharyngeal/oropharyngeal (NP/OP) swabs were collected at admission. Blood specimens were cultured for bacteria, and a blood slide was prepared to determine malaria infection status. Blood samples were analyzed with a complete blood count [WBC, red blood cell counts (RBC), platelets, neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils]. The biomarker discovery study tested the blood samples from a subset of children and quantified 418 plasma proteins using high-performance liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (HPLC-MS/MS) [11]. CRP and 6 other plasma proteins appeared predictive of infectious aetiology: angiotensinogen (AGT), Serpin Family A Member 1 (SERPINA1), Serpin Family A Member 3 (SERPINA3), Paraoxonase-1 (PON1), Histidine Rich Glycoprotein (HRG/B2R8I2), and lipopolysaccharide-binding protein (LBP) [11] and were therefore considered for etiology differentiation for this study. Samples from the whole cohort of children were then tested for CRP, PCT, and these 6 novel proteins using the same mass spectrometry. The ILab Aries clinical biochemistry analyzer was used to measure a subset of 100 CRP samples, which were converted to concentrations (8). Using the training dataset, excluding children with infections of unknown aetiology and bacterial-viral co-infections, the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve was used to identify optimal cutoff points for the mean fluorescent intensity (MFI) values of biomarkers, enabling categorization into categorical variables with the highest sensitivity, specificity, and overall discriminatory ability. These derived cut-offs from the training set were then applied unchanged to the validation dataset. Further exploratory analyses to determine cut-off points for biomarkers were also identified by stratifying the dataset by age (<1 and ≥1 years, <2 and ≥2 years, and <3 and ≥3 years) on the entire dataset to assess whether cut-offs varied by age, as this has been reported in some previous literature (26). The variable with the lower AUC was dropped. Exploratory interaction analyses were conducted after the primary analyses to assess whether an interaction between pneumonia severity and the eight biomarkers, adjusting for age, could explain the biomarkers’ performance. full_text_sections.results: ResultsAmong the 457 children enrolled in this study, 228 (49.9%) had NP/OP swabs PCR + for viral infections known to cause pneumonia and no evidence of other infections, 93 (20.4%) had a positive blood culture for a bacterial infection, 12 (2.6%) had a bacterial-viral co-infection, and 124 (27.1%) had unknown etiology (i.e., negative blood culture, negative PCR panel, negative malaria slide; Figure 1). Among the 228 with a viral infection, the most identified viral pathogens were RSV-A (n = 39, 17.1%), parainfluenza-3 (n = 36, 15.8%), human metapneumovirus (n = 35, 15.4%), influenza-A (n = 34, 14.9%), and adenovirus (n = 28, 12.3%). The most identified bacterial pathogens from blood cultures were Escherichia coli (n = 17, 7.4%), Streptococcus pneumoniae (n = 17, 7.4%), Staphylococcus aureus (n = 11, 4.8%), and Haemophilus influenzae (n = 8, 3.5%). (Supplementary Figures S1, S2).Demographic, laboratory, and clinical characteristicsMore than half (63%) of the study population had severe pneumonia compared to (non-severe) pneumonia (37%) (Supplementary Table S2). A higher proportion of children with probable viral pneumonia presented with severe pneumonia (72%), compared to children with possible bacterial pneumonia (54%) (Supplementary Table S2). Cell counts of WBC (p-value = 0.002), neutrophils (p-value = 0.017), and the median fluorescent intensity (MFI) units of AGT (p-value = 0.002), LBP (p-value = 0.005), PCT (p-value = 0.020), and SERPINA1 (p-value = 0.002) were significantly higher in the bacterial group, while the cell counts of RBC (p-value = 0.014), hemoglobin (p-value = 0.029) concentrations, and MFI units of SERPINA3 (p-value = 0.014) were significantly higher in the viral group (Supplementary Table S1).Predictive capacity of each biomarker to differentiate bacterial from viral infectionsBased on this nested study's case definition, AGT had the best discriminatory power (AUC = 0.60, 95% CI [0.53, 0.66]), followed by PCT (AUC = 0.58, 95% CI [0.52, 0.64]) and SERPINA1 (AUC = 0.58, 95% CI [0.52, 0.64]), and lastly LBP (AUC = 0.56, 95% CI [0.50, 0.63] (Table 1)). CRP, HRG, PON1, and SERPINA3 could not distinguish bacterial from viral infections beyond chance as their confidence intervals had limits below 0.50 (Table S1). Assessing the biomarker performance on ‘pure’ bacterial and viral infections of pneumonia, AGT (AUC = 0.76, 95% CI [0.69, 0.83]) had the highest discriminatory power, followed by PCT (AUC = 0.65, 95% CI [0.57, 0.73]), LBP (AUC = 0.65, 95% CI [0.56, 0.73]), and SERPINA1 (AUC = 0.65, 95% CI [0.56, 0.73]) while SERPINA3 (AUC = 0.56, 95% CI [0.48, 0.65]) and HRG (AUC = 0.57, 95% CI [0.49, 0.65]) could not discriminate beyond chance (Supplementary Table S5). There was a high degree of overlap observed across the bacterial and viral biomarker levels (Figure 2). full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionIn this nested case-control study, we utilized a dataset containing data on a wide range of clinical signs and symptoms, complete blood cell counts, CRP, PCT and 6 novel biomarker levels to develop a multivariable predictive model and evaluate its ability to discriminate between bacterial and viral pneumonia in children presenting with WHO-defined pneumonia. The model incorporated some novel biomarkers, which have not been assessed for this purpose before, to evaluate their incremental value in predicting etiology and to account for any underlying biological pathways not captured by conventional biomarkers. The majority of study participants were severely ill, reflecting the severe case mix presenting to the hospital in Kilifi, and more broadly, sub-Saharan Africa (24, 25), where morbidity is underpinned by poverty, malnutrition, and inaccessibility to healthcare facilities.In age-adjusted analyses, higher MFI units of AGT, LBP, and SERPINA1 were associated with increased probability of an individual having bacterial pneumonia. However, neither biomarker remained significantly predictive of bacterial infections after controlling for age and chest-wall indrawing. In internal validation, the final model, including age and LCWI, lacked sufficient predictive power to guide clinical decision-making (AUC = 0.61, 95% CI [0.52, 0.70], sensitivity = 0.50, specificity = 0.68). Performing internal validation indicated that the predictions were overly extreme (potential model overfit), whereas the training set was well calibrated. This is consistent with the internal cross-validation model performance, which had a mean AUC of 0.64, indicating that model development performance was optimistic (AUC = 0.72), with overestimation on unseen observations. When we performed sensitivity analyses excluding participants with unknown etiology, model performance improved. This model, which included chest-wall indrawing, cough, crackles, and AGT (>=7.9144) and was adjusted for age, achieved an AUC of 0.91. These findings suggest that including participants with unknown infections may have attenuated the model's ability to distinguish bacterial from viral pneumonia.Other published models developed for the same purpose have reported equally poor performance on internal validation. The performance of these models did not improve when we externally validated them on our dataset. The study by Farida et al. (15) was conducted in a population with a similar age group and case mix to our population. However, their outcome of interest was defined differently from ours as they excluded unknown infections. Despite this, their model performed just as badly on our population as in their own internal validation. The model identified by Bhuiyan et al. (9), despite having moderate discrimination in our study population (AUC = 0.74), lacks sufficient sensitivity to guide clinical decision-making (sensitivity = 0.55).Differentiating bacterial from viral pneumonia remains a challenge. Incorporating novel biomarker levels in our study did not improve predictive performance compared with other models that included only clinical and demographic data. The distribution of MFI units significantly overlapped in bacterial and viral cases. To explore possible reasons why, after controlling for age and LCWI, biomarker levels were not predictive, we assessed interactions between biomarkers’ predictive capacity and pneumonia severity, adjusting forage. CRP, AGT, HRG, and SERPINA1 had significant interactions with pneumonia severity; higher values were more predictive of pneumonia etiology in non-severe cases than in severe cases (supplementary Table S8), as also reported by Wu et al. (26), who noted that CRP was significantly associated with severe pneumonia and therefore suboptimal as a stand-alone predictor. Other studies have found that levels of SERPINA1, PON1, and LBP are higher in bacterial infections and can identify patients with CAP among other patients (7, 19, 27–30), however, these markers do not adequately differentiate between bacterial and viral etiologies. HRG has been shown to exert an antifungal effect, and its levels negatively correlate with disease severity (31). Previous studies have reported interactions between CRP and age and LBP and age (16, 32–34). We assessed each biomarker using different cut-offs for different ages; however, this did not significantly improve their predictive capacity.This analysis, as with others before it, has notable strengths and limitations. The strengths include: a representative sample of 457 pediatric hospital admissions, with biological samples which were tested for a wide range of bacterial and viral pathogens known to cause pneumonia at a world-class research laboratory. The available data on possible predictors included a wide panel of novel and conventional biomarkers (eight, 8) along with over 20 clinical signs and symptoms (25). Despite these strengths, we acknowledge that a major limitation is probable outcome misclassification: 54% of the children included in the possible bacterial group had an unknown etiology, with a negative blood culture and negative PCR for all tested viral targets. This is a direct result of the insensitivity of bacterial cultures and the specificity required by PCR (6, 35). Although bacterial culture is the gold standard for identifying bacterial infections, it is insensitive due to contamination, prior antibiotic therapy, and infections existing in inaccessible sites (32, 35). Furthermore, the PCR testing panel that was used to define viral pneumonia identified 11 respiratory pathogens. However, there are other viruses known to cause pneumonia-related hospitalizations, such as human bocavirus, which were not on the PCR testing panel. The viral infection outcome was identified from NP/OP swabs, which is only a proxy for the site of infection in the lungs, potentially leading to outcome misclassification.An additional limitation of this analysis is that the laboratory biomarker levels were recorded as MFI units. Although internally valid, this limits the study's replicability, generalizability, and direct comparability to other studies that report their levels and biomarker thresholds as concentrations. Lastly, although our study cohort is representative of pediatric hospital admissions, a large amount of antimicrobial use occurs in outpatient settings, and our findings cannot be generalized to outpatient care.ConclusionDistinguishing between bacterial and viral cases of childhood pneumonia in sub-Saharan Africa remains a challenge. This analysis follows the widespread administration of the PCV and Hib vaccines in Kenya; in this context, the case mix presentating to the hospital is increasingly of viral etiology and therefore would not benefit from antibiotics. However, in our analysis, which included all children presenting with WHO-defined pneumonia or severe pneumonia, including infections of unknown etiology, we still could not identify a group of predictors that can accurately identify bacterial infections with enough sensitivity and specificity to guide clinical decision-making. Our study has demonstrated that biomarker performance is affected by disease severity and thresholds could differ with age. Further research addressing some of the limitations we encountered in outcome classification, stratifying by disease severity and potentially accounting for variation in biomarker performance by age, may improve predictions.

full_text_sections.other: IntroductionGlobally, the incidence of pneumonia in the pediatric population has significantly decreased following the widespread administration of pneumococcal conjugate vaccines (PCVs) and Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) vaccines (1, 2). However, pneumonia remains one of the leading causes of pediatric morbidity and mortality, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. As bacterial infections have decreased, severe viral infections now account for a larger proportion of the hospital caseload (1, 3). Guidelines still recommend the empirical use of antibiotics, as this has been instrumental in preventing bacterial infection-related deaths; however, it is thought that unnecessary use of antibiotics for viral infections has inadvertently fueled antimicrobial resistance (AMR) (4, 5). Diagnostic tools to guide the rational use of antibiotics in the treatment of pneumonia are needed.The distinction between bacterial and viral pneumonia remains challenging, especially in Low- and Middle-Income countries (LMICs). An accurate distinction between bacterial and viral pathogens is crucial for guiding antibiotic treatment (5). However, conventional methods to identify bacterial infection, such as blood and sputum cultures, are invasive, have limited sensitivity, and are time-consuming (6, 7). Meanwhile, molecular testing, such as Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) (6, 7), provides higher sensitivities and specificities, but is expensive and only detects specific pathogens. Transcriptomics has been used to accurately distinguish bacterial from viral pneumonia with high sensitivity and specificity (8, 9); however, it remains impractical in LMICs due to its high cost and the need for advanced laboratory infrastructure (9).Scalable and more affordable methods to distinguish bacterial pneumonia from viral pneumonia remain elusive (10, 11). Individuals with bacterial pneumonia and those with viral pneumonia present with overlapping clinical signs and symptoms and biomarker levels making the use of individual symptoms or concentrations of solitary markers suboptimal (12–14). Concentrations of biomarkers such as C-reactive protein (CRP) and procalcitonin (PCT), have in the past been significantly higher in bacterial pneumonia compared to viral pneumonia cases (15). However, these biomarkers had low sensitivities (CRP = 0.70, PCT = 0.66). The biomarker discovery study tested the blood samples from a subset of children and quantified 418 plasma proteins using high-performance liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (HPLC-MS/MS) [11]. papers.title_original: Predictive modelling to differentiate possible bacterial and viral cases of childhood pneumonia in Kilifi, Kenya using protein markers and clinical data

analysis.research_question_and_background: We aimed to incorporate a wide range of novel biomarkers and clinical presentations into a multivariable model and to validate its ability to differentiate bacterial from viral pneumonia.MethodsA total of 457 children aged 2–59 months, admitted to the Kilifi County Referral Hospital, Kenya, with WHO defined pneumonia were classified using gold standard laboratory diagnostics as possible bacterial (i.e., bacterial/ unknown cases, n = 229) or possible viral (n = 228) infections.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The most identified bacterial pathogens from blood cultures were Escherichia coli (n = 17, 7.4%), Streptococcus pneumoniae (n = 17, 7.4%), Staphylococcus aureus (n = 11, 4.8%), and Haemophilus influenzae (n = 8, 3.5%).
analysis.methods: DiscussionIn this nested case-control study, we utilized a dataset containing data on a wide range of clinical signs and symptoms, complete blood cell counts, CRP, PCT and 6 novel biomarker levels to develop a multivariable predictive model and evaluate its ability to discriminate between bacterial and viral pneumonia in children presenting with WHO-defined pneumonia.
analysis.main_results: This model demonstrated good discrimination, with an Area Under the Curve of 0.78 on the validation dataset.ConclusionAmong children admitted to the hospital with WHO-defined pneumonia, modelling a wide range of biomarkers and clinical presentations still failed to distinguish bacterial from viral pneumonia with enough accuracy to guide clinical management.

analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: This analysis follows the widespread administration of the PCV and Hib vaccines in Kenya; in this context, the case mix presentating to the hospital is increasingly of viral etiology and therefore would not benefit from antibiotics.

analysis.summary_en: We aimed to incorporate a wide range of novel biomarkers and clinical presentations into a multivariable model and to validate its ability to differentiate bacterial from viral pneumonia.MethodsA total of 457 children aged 2–59 months, admitted to the Kilifi County Referral Hospital, Kenya, with WHO defined pneumonia were classified using gold standard laboratory diagnostics as possible bacterial (i.e., bacterial/ unknown cases, n = 229) or possible viral (n = 228) infections. DiscussionIn this nested case-control study, we utilized a dataset containing data on a wide range of clinical signs and symptoms, complete blood cell counts, CRP, PCT and 6 novel biomarker levels to develop a multivariable predictive model and evaluate its ability to discriminate between bacterial and viral pneumonia in children presenting with WHO-defined pneumonia. This model demonstrated good discrimination, with an Area Under the Curve of 0.78 on the validation dataset.ConclusionAmong children admitted to the hospital with WHO-defined pneumonia, modelling a wide range of biomarkers and clinical presentations still failed to distinguish bacterial from viral pneumonia with enough accuracy to guide clinical management. elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 我们的目的是将广泛的新型生物标志物和临床表现纳入多变量模型,并验证其区分细菌性肺炎和病毒性肺炎的能力。方法使用金标准实验室诊断将肯尼亚基利菲县转诊医院收治的总共 457 名 2-59 个月大、患有 WHO 定义的肺炎的儿童分类为可能的细菌(即细菌/未知病例,n = 229)或可能的病毒(n = 228)感染。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: The most identified bacterial pathogens from blood cultures were Escherichia coli (n = 17, 7.4%), Streptococcus pneumoniae (n = 17, 7.4%), Staphylococcus aureus (n = 11, 4.8%), and Haemophilus influenzae (n = 8, 3.5%).
elements_zh.methods: 讨论在这项嵌套病例对照研究中,我们利用包含各种临床体征和症状、全血细胞计数、CRP、PCT 和 6 种新型生物标志物水平数据的数据集来开发多变量预测模型,并评估其区分患有 WHO 定义的肺炎的儿童细菌性肺炎和病毒性肺炎的能力。
elements_zh.main_results: 该模型表现出良好的区分度,验证数据集上的曲线下面积为 0.78。结论 在因 WHO 定义的肺炎入院的儿童中,对各种生物标志物和临床表现进行建模仍然无法以足够的准确性区分细菌性肺炎和病毒性肺炎,以指导临床管理。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 该模型展示了公平但不充分的歧视,曲线下面积为 0.61。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 需要诊断工具来指导在肺炎中合理使用抗生素。细菌性肺炎和病毒性肺炎之间的区别仍然具有挑战性,特别是在低收入和中等收入国家 (LMIC)。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本分析是在肯尼亚广泛施用 PCV 和 Hib 疫苗 后进行的;在这种情况下,向医院提出的病例组合越来越多地是由病毒引起的,因此不会从抗生素中受益。
